value.overview: The Least Tern (Sternula antillarum) is the smallest tern in North America and one of the smallest marine terns in the world. It is a slender, highly maneuverable bird that breeds in colonies on open sandy or gravelly ground and feeds mainly by plunge-diving for small fish. Adults are pale gray and white with narrow pointed wings, a forked tail, and a distinctive black-and-white head pattern during the breeding season.
value.classification: The Least Tern belongs to the order Charadriiformes and the gull-and-tern family Laridae. Several regional subspecies are recognized, including coastal, interior, and California populations.
value.identification: This very small tern measures about 21–23 cm long, with a wingspan of roughly 48–53 cm. Breeding adults have a pale gray back, white underparts, a black crown, white forehead, yellow bill often marked with a dark tip, and yellowish legs. Nonbreeding adults have a darker bill, a less sharply defined crown, and sometimes a dark wing bar. In flight, its narrow pointed wings, rapid jerky wingbeats, and deeply forked tail are characteristic.
value.rangeHabitat: Least Terns breed along much of the Atlantic, Gulf, and Pacific coasts of North America, as well as locally along major inland rivers and lakes. They use sandy beaches, shell banks, barrier islands, river islands, mudflats, dredged material, gravel pits, and occasionally flat gravel roofs. In Costa Rica, the species is a rare or occasional visitor rather than a regular breeding bird. Records are associated mainly with coastal waters, beaches, estuaries, bays, and river mouths, especially during passage or the nonbreeding season.
value.migrationStatus: A long-distance migrant. North American breeders move south after nesting, with many wintering along tropical American coasts and in northern South America. In Costa Rica, it is uncommon and recorded irregularly during migration or the nonbreeding period; it is not considered a resident species or established breeder there.
value.breeding: Least Terns nest colonially in open, sparsely vegetated places close to shallow feeding water. The nest is usually a shallow scrape in sand, shell, gravel, or bare soil, sometimes lined with small pebbles or shell fragments. Both adults defend the nest area and care for the young. Courtship includes aerial displays and the male's presentation of small fish to the female. Nesting success can be strongly affected by flooding, predators, storms, and human disturbance.
value.dietFeeding: The diet consists primarily of small fish caught by plunge-diving in shallow coastal or inland waters. A Least Tern often hovers briefly before dropping into the water, and it may carry fish to a mate or chick. It also occasionally takes shrimp, tadpoles, aquatic insects, and other small invertebrates. Feeding habitats include ocean shores, bays, estuaries, lagoons, rivers, ponds, and reservoirs.
value.behavior: Least Terns are fast, agile, and highly vocal, particularly around nesting colonies. Their flight is direct, with stiff, rapid wingbeats, and they frequently hover before diving. Adults defend nest sites with alarm calls and attack flights directed at predators or intruders. Outside the breeding season they gather in flocks, forage along shorelines and river mouths, and may rest on beaches, sandbars, mudflats, pilings, or other exposed surfaces.

conservation.populationTrend: The global population trend is generally regarded as decreasing, with substantial declines documented in North American monitoring programs. Trends vary among regional populations, and the species remains locally common in some areas while declining or becoming scarce in others.
conservation.threats: Major threats include loss and alteration of open nesting beaches, coastal development, recreational disturbance, trampling of nests, shoreline stabilization, altered river flows, flooding, predators, severe storms, and reduced availability of small fish. In Costa Rica, occasional birds may be affected by disturbance or habitat degradation at coastal feeding and roosting sites, although the country is not a major breeding area for the species.
conservation.howToHelp: Protect open beaches, sandbars, estuaries, and river-mouth habitats used by resting and foraging terns. Keep people, vehicles, and dogs away from marked bird colonies and roosts, especially during the nesting season. Support coastal conservation, responsible fisheries, and monitoring programs, and report sightings through established bird-recording platforms without approaching or disturbing the birds.
